name: Pioneer Lunar Program (1958-1959)
short_status: A completed, mostly failed campaign, Aug 1958 to Mar 1959: five lunar probes, four failures and one partial success. None reached the Moon; only Pioneer 4 escaped Earth's gravity, and it still circles the Sun today.
tagline: ARPA, USAF, NASA and Army-JPL · United States · Programme · 1958 · The space race Partial
stats: lunar probes launched in seven months, four outright failures and one partial success
reached escape velocity: Pioneer 4, the first US craft to leave Earth's gravity
Pioneer 1 peak altitude, a record at the time but only about a third of the way to the Moon
Pioneer 4 lunar flyby distance, about twice too far to trigger its Moon sensor

facts.label: Pioneer 0 (Thor-Able 1)
facts.value: Launched 17 Aug 1958, 12:18 UT from Cape Canaveral; the first US lunar attempt and the first attempted launch beyond Earth orbit by any nation. The Thor first stage exploded about 77 seconds after liftoff at roughly 16 km altitude. An Air Force / ARPA mission: NASA did not yet exist.

facts.label: Pioneer 1
facts.value: Launched 11 Oct 1958, 08:42:13 UT on a Thor-Able; NASA's very first spacecraft, flown 10 days after the agency opened. An upper-stage error left it on a ballistic arc peaking at 113,800 km; it reentered over the South Pacific on 13 Oct 1958 at 03:46 UT after about 43 hours.

facts.label: Pioneer 2
facts.value: Launched 8 Nov 1958, 07:30:21 UT on a Thor-Able; the third stage separated but never ignited. Reached only 1,550 km before reentering over northwest Africa. It returned a small amount of data on near-Earth radiation and micrometeorites.

facts.label: Pioneer 3
facts.value: Launched 6 Dec 1958, 05:45 UT on a Juno II by the Army Ballistic Missile Agency with NASA; a 5.87 kg cone-shaped JPL probe. Its first stage cut off about 3.7 seconds early, so it fell short at 102,360 km altitude and reentered over Africa on 7 Dec 1958.

facts.label: Pioneer 3's real prize
facts.value: Its two Geiger-Mueller tubes (James Van Allen's experiment) sampled the radiation on the way up and on the way down, and the data showed the trapped radiation was structured as two distinct belts, helping establish the existence of a second, outer Van Allen radiation belt.

facts.label: Pioneer 4
facts.value: Launched 3 Mar 1959, 05:10:56 UT on a Juno II; the first US spacecraft to reach escape velocity and enter heliocentric orbit. It passed within about 60,000 km of the Moon on 4 Mar 1959 at 22:25 UT at 7,230 km/hr, was tracked to 655,000 km, and reached perihelion on 18 Mar 1959.

facts.label: Why Pioneer 4 is only a partial success
facts.value: Its photoelectric sensor was designed to trigger a radiation and imaging sequence only within about 30,000 km of the Moon. Pioneer 4 flew by at roughly twice that distance, so the sensor never fired and no lunar photography was obtained; no lunar radiation was detected either.

facts.label: Two programs, one name
facts.value: Pioneer 0, 1, and 2 were ~34 to 39 kg Able probes built by Space Technology Laboratories (later TRW) and flown on Thor-Able for the Air Force, then NASA. Pioneer 3 and 4 were tiny ~6 kg JPL cones flown on Juno II for the Army. They share a name but almost no hardware.

facts.label: The intended missions
facts.value: The Air Force Able probes aimed to enter lunar orbit (Pioneer 0 targeted a ~29,000 km orbit) carrying an infrared imaging scanner; the Army/JPL probes were flyby craft meant to pass close to the Moon and continue into solar orbit. None achieved its full plan.

facts.label: NASA's opening act
facts.value: NASA began operations on 1 Oct 1958, inheriting the Air Force lunar-probe effort. Pioneer 1, launched 11 Oct 1958, was therefore the first spacecraft flown under NASA, even though its rocket and probe had been built by an Air Force contractor.

facts.label: Records set
facts.value: Pioneer 1's 113,800 km was the greatest distance any human-made object had reached from Earth at that date. Pioneer 4 then became the first American probe to break free of Earth entirely and, as of decades later, was still orbiting the Sun.

timeline: Pioneer 0 (Thor-Able 1) lifts off from Cape Canaveral, the first US Moon attempt; the Thor first stage explodes about 77 seconds into flight over the Atlantic
NASA opens for business and takes over the Air Force lunar-probe program
Pioneer 1, NASA's first spacecraft, launches on a Thor-Able; an upper-stage error caps it at 113,800 km, then it falls back and reenters over the South Pacific on 13 Oct
Pioneer 2 launches on a Thor-Able; the third stage fails to ignite and the probe peaks at just 1,550 km before reentering over northwest Africa
Pioneer 3 launches on a Juno II for the Army and NASA; a premature engine cutoff strands it at 102,360 km, but its Geiger tubes reveal a second, outer Van Allen belt before it reenters on 7 Dec
Pioneer 4 launches on a Juno II and becomes the first US spacecraft to reach escape velocity and leave Earth's gravity
Pioneer 4 passes within about 60,000 km of the Moon at 22:25 UT, too far out to trigger its photoelectric sensor, then continues into solar orbit
Pioneer 4 reaches perihelion, confirmed in a heliocentric orbit; the program's only craft to escape Earth, and its final flight
